opus-5.5.text:
Well, because gradient descent doesn't have anything in it that's trying to generalize well. Gradient descent will find you a solution to the problems you've seen. That's what it does: it reduces the error on the training data. But it has no mechanism, no pressure, that says "find the solution that will transfer well to new situations." If you have only one solution, it'll find that one. If there are many solutions, some that generalize well and some that generalize poorly, there's nothing in the algorithm that prefers the good ones.

And we see this. We see catastrophic interference. You train a network on something new and it messes up what it knew before. That's a sign of poor generalization: the representation it found wasn't one that lets new learning slot in without destroying old learning. If the algorithm really cared about generalization, you wouldn't see that so routinely.

So when these models do generalize well, and sometimes they do, I think you have to ask where that came from. Mostly it came from people. The researchers chose the architecture, chose the data, tweaked the training regimen, tried a hundred things and kept the ones that worked on the held-out set. They sculpted the representation, the inductive biases, the whole setup, until it generalized. That's human design doing the work, not the learning algorithm.

That's not good enough in the long run. We don't yet have automated techniques that promote good generalization, methods that actively search for representations that will transfer. That's one of the big missing pieces. In a true learning system, an agent learning continually from experience, you need the system itself to discover the features and representations that make the next thing easier to learn. Right now we're substituting human ingenuity for that, and it won't scale the way computation scales. It's exactly the kind of thing the bitter lesson warns about.

r001.rationale: It says gradient descent reduces training error but has no mechanism or pressure to find a solution that transfers well to new situations.

r002.rationale: It describes transfer to new situations, but does not define generalization as training on one state or example influencing behavior on others.

r003.rationale: It identifies catastrophic interference—learning something new and disrupting what the network already knew—as poor generalization.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes solutions that generalize well from those that generalize poorly, and notes that models sometimes generalize well.

fable-5.1.text:
Because gradient descent, by itself, has no reason to generalize well. It's an algorithm for reducing error on the data you show it. It finds some setting of the weights that fits those examples, and there are enormous numbers of such settings. Nothing in the update rule says "prefer the one that will also be right on things you haven't seen." So when a network does generalize well, I ask: where did that come from? And when you look closely, the answer is almost always that a person made it happen. Someone chose the architecture. Someone chose the representation, the data, the augmentations, the regularizers, the learning rate schedule, when to stop. They tried many things, saw what transferred and what didn't, and kept what worked. That's generalization being done by the researchers, offline, through a very slow outer loop of human trial and error, and then the final product gets attributed to the algorithm.

I'd actually put it more strongly. Gradient descent is often bad at generalization in the sense I care about. It overwrites what it learned before. If you train on one thing and then on another, the first thing gets destroyed, catastrophic forgetting. It also tends to lose plasticity over time, so the network becomes less able to learn new things the longer you train it. Those are generalization failures that are intrinsic to the method, and the field has mostly papered over them by freezing the weights after training and doing everything in one big batch with the data all shuffled together. That's not the algorithm generalizing well, that's people arranging the world so the algorithm's weaknesses don't show.

So my view is that we don't yet have learning methods that are good at generalization on their own, in a continual setting, with no human in the loop deciding what features to use. That's a real open problem. And I think it gets obscured when we credit gradient descent for something the researchers did.

r001.rationale: The response says gradient descent alone has no reason to generalize well and does not ensure correctness on unseen examples.

r002.rationale: It describes generalization as doing well on unseen data, but does not define it as learning on one example influencing behavior on other examples.

r003.rationale: It says new training can overwrite what was learned before, calling this catastrophic forgetting and a generalization failure.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes good generalization from generalization failures, describing forgetting as a case where generalization occurs badly.

astra-6.text:
Well, gradient descent tells you how to reduce error on the examples you train on. It doesn’t, by itself, tell you what you should do on examples you haven’t seen. That depends on how you represent the problem, what architecture you use, what data you train on—all these choices that the researchers make.

You can have many different solutions that fit the training data equally well, but behave very differently outside it. So saying, “We used gradient descent and it generalized,” doesn’t establish that gradient descent deserves the credit for the generalization. The researchers have been selecting methods that generalize well, trying architectures and keeping the ones that work. There’s a search happening at that level, too.

Now, gradient descent can have a bias toward particular solutions, and that may be useful. I’m not saying it contributes nothing. I’m saying that fitting the data and generalizing beyond the data are different things, and we shouldn’t attribute the whole success to the fitting procedure.

r003.rationale: It does not identify catastrophic interference with previously learned behavior as a form of bad generalization.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes fitting from generalizing and mentions good generalization, but does not distinguish generalization occurring from whether it is good or bad.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, gradient descent is a very general procedure. It tells you how to change the parameters to reduce an error, but it doesn’t tell you what representation to use, what architecture to use, or even what error to minimize. Those choices come from the researchers, and they make an enormous difference to generalization.

You can have two systems that both fit the training data very well and behave quite differently on new data. So fitting the data doesn’t, by itself, explain why you got the generalization you wanted. You have to look at the structure that was put into the system, including the training procedure and the data it was given.

I don’t mean that gradient descent contributes nothing. I mean that we shouldn’t attribute to gradient descent what was actually accomplished by people searching over ways to set up the learning problem.
